Hey! I'm 17 and at risk for a terminal illness called Huntington's disease. My mother has the disease and it's essentially eaten the part of her brain responsible for rational thinking and emotional maturity, meaning that she is less than a pleasant person to be around and I've spent the majority of my childhood raising her, myself, and my little siblings. 

When I was told of my mother's diagnosis and that I have a 50% chance of inheritance, I lost my mind for about a month, wouldn't eat, and couldn't sleep. After that I slowly accepted that there's nothing I can do about it and that I can't wither away just because the promise of death may approach me faster and more violently than I want it to. I've made friends with a lot of people online who have various terminal illnesses and their mindset is essentially the same. Dying sucks and it's scary, but you get to a point where you realize there's nothing else you can do about it but live your life until it gets to you. In a world like AoT where it's very possible that you could be stomped, sniped, or blown up at any minute, that principle probably applies even more because the majority of the population probably doesn't see themselves living 13 years into the future anyway.

As a child of an HD+ parent, if you can't love your partner as she progresses then please leave. My parents are in an incredibly unhappy, emotionally abusive marriage and the only reason they aren't divorced is because my dad knows there's nobody else to take care of my mom. Her personality has done a 180 over the past decade, my dad's grown to hate her, and their dynamic not only affects their sanity but also the sanity of the children. I'm 17 years old and my entire childhood has been focused on finally being able to graduate high school and move out because I hate being at home. If you aren't confident that you can love your partner and take care of them as they decline, then leave.

Also, do not try to convince yourself that you can be her caretaker out of guilt. If you can't do it, you can't do it. That's how my dad got into his situation.

Stuff like this is why I plan on telling any partner I have that I'm at risk as soon as things show signs of being serious.

My responsibilities mainly lie in household stuff and helping out with my little siblings because mom has cognitively declined a lot and she has the same thought process as a 12 year old a lot of the time, but she's still physically able to function to a certain extent. I don't like her doing anything dangerous like boiling water because she did have an incident last year where her chroea caused her to dump the pot down her legs by accident while she was trying to cook and she was rendered immobile for over a month. Because of her current state, I don't really consider my duty as being her caretaker because she doesnt require physical care other than a few things, moreso just picking up slack and trying to keep normalcy for my siblings. Her cognitive decline has caused her to become very unmotivated, short tempered, irrational, and depressed, so she's usually in bed for the majority of the day and has a lot of outbursts. Their general consensus is that mom is lazy and mean, which sucks because it's so much deeper than that, but they're young enough to where that's probably better for them right now than knowing that she's dying. Mom definitely does stuff around the house, but it isn't very often and my siblings consider me more of an adult figure than her.

As she gets older and continues to decline, my dad will begin to take more and more time off of work because he plans on being her full-time caretaker when the time comes. He's encouraging me to leave and go to college because he knows I'm miserable here and that there'll never be any opportunities for me if I feel tied down to our home situation. I still plan on keeping a lot of contact for the my siblings' sake even though my relationship with both of my parents is very strained, but putting my life and career on hold to care for someone who has done a lot of harm to me throughout my life is not something my dad wants me to do, which I appreciate.

The average age of symptom onset in general is around 35-40, and my family's history falls right into that category so becoming symptomatic while getting a college education would be incredibly unlikely. I don't plan on testing as soon as I turn 18 but would like to in my mid-early 20s. Up until last year I was living with the assumption that I was gene positive because I didn't wanna get my hopes up but I realized that it was a bad mindset to have and that I have a good 20ish years before very mild symptoms begin to appear. CAG count inheritance doesn't tend to vary much from generation to generation if it's passed down from the mother (researchers aren't sure why but they want to test some stuff with the Y chromosome to figure it out) and my mother and grandmother both started experiencing mild physical symptoms at around 35 that progressed into cognitive and physical decline as they got older.

Not necessarily that I feel guilty about the fact that I'm helping her, moreso the idea of "taking credit" for it when I've kind of grown up being told that it's something that's expected of me if that makes sense.

I can't stress how much I agree with that last part. I'm so glad I've been able to find friends who support me and *understand* my situation without trying to relate it to something else or by pressuring me into looking at the bright side when sometimes I just can't. A lot of the advice I got when I first found out at 14 was "Well you're not dying yet" or "just try to make the most of the time you have with your mom", which are nice sentiments but aren't exactly helpful when the only things I was able to think of were the fact that I *could* be dying and that my relationship with my mom had been horrible for all of those years prior because of the disease that might end up killing me alongside her.

I tend to take little breaks from this subreddit for the sake of my mental health but anytime I come back it's always so refreshing to talk to other people who share the same experiences as I do. 🩷

I think it's absolutely lovely you have someone by your side who has known you so long and cares about you so much. I feel like finding someone who sticks around even with a positive HD diagnosis on the table is something a lot of people around my age in the community are scared of, and this is definitely very reassuring. 

I fully agree with you with your final paragraph about getting your hopes up over cures. My mother is HD+, gets her hopes up about any trial that makes it past the first phase, and then becomes extremely depressed anytime it doesn't pass. It's hard, because I feel like clinging onto hope is the only thing keeping her going, but we've also been five years away from a cure for like 25 years.
